list.title: RAG Document Assistant
list.descProject: A document-grounded assistant built with Next.js, FastAPI and PostgreSQL/pgvector. It extracts text from PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD files, splits it page by page, embeds it with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, then retrieves, LLM-reranks and answers with deduplicated page-level sources through a documented REST API.

description.title: What I built
points: Accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD uploads with a 50 MB limit and explicit format validation.
Preserves exact page numbers during pypdf/python-docx extraction and RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter chunking.
Embeds chunks in batches of 100 with text-embedding-3-small and stores them in a pgvector HNSW cosine index.
Retrieves 20 candidates, reranks them with gpt-4o-mini structured scoring, then sends the top 5 passages to the answer model.
Returns structured answers with deduplicated document, page, excerpt and similarity-score sources; when context is insufficient, the model leaves sources empty and says so.
Exposes /health, document list/upload/delete and /api/chat endpoints with a Next.js 14 chat UI and document selector.

devopsProcess.title: Delivery & checks
steps: Runs PostgreSQL/pgvector, the FastAPI backend and the Next.js frontend as three Docker Compose services.
Creates the vector extension, tables and HNSW index on startup with a bounded psycopg connection pool.
Keeps model choice, chunk size, retrieval depth, reranking, CORS and upload limit in a documented .env template.
Uses Pydantic settings and response schemas so configuration errors and API contracts fail early.
Adds health checks, upload-size validation and explicit 400/413/500 error paths for operational clarity.
Documents local and Docker workflows, curl examples and troubleshooting steps in the repository README.

list.summary: Document-grounded RAG assistant with page-level citations, LLM reranking and a FastAPI + Next.js stack.

citation.name: Janet Williams
citation.citation: Computer science is more than just lines of code. It's the expression of creativity, problem-solving, and building a digital future.

blogList.title: MCP and Agentic Interoperability in 2026: Connecting Models to Real Tools Safely

desc.title: Why interoperability became the agent problem
desc.description: As AI agents moved from chat to action, the bottleneck shifted from model capability to integration. Every tool had its own API, auth model, schema, and failure behavior. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerged as an open way to expose tools, resources, and prompts through a consistent interface. In 2026, the value is not hype: it is reducing bespoke glue code while making tool boundaries explicit.
list: Tools: callable actions with typed inputs and outputs.
Resources: readable context such as docs, tickets, or records.
Prompts/workflows: reusable task templates exposed by servers.
Permissions: user and host control over what an agent can access.

desc.title: A simple MCP mental model
desc.description: An MCP host runs the agent experience. It connects to MCP servers, discovers capabilities, and calls them with structured input. The model decides when to use a capability, but the host and server enforce boundaries. This separation is important: model reasoning is probabilistic; authorization and data access must be deterministic.

desc.title: Security boundaries still matter
desc.description: A standard protocol does not remove security work. MCP servers should authenticate callers, scope access, validate inputs, log audits, and avoid exposing overly broad tools. Hosts should require user confirmation for sensitive actions and isolate untrusted tool output from system instructions. Prompt injection through retrieved content remains a real threat model in 2026.
desc.note: Treat tool descriptions and external content as untrusted data. The model can read them, but your policy layer should decide what actions are allowed.

desc.title: Where MCP fits in real architectures
desc.description: MCP is useful when multiple clients or agents need the same internal capabilities: documentation search, issue tracking, CI status, database read models, or cloud operations. It is less useful when a single app needs one private API call. Good engineering chooses protocols for interoperability and governance, not because they are new.

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: Agentic interoperability is becoming infrastructure. Protocols like MCP help, but the science and engineering challenge remains the same: reliable tool use, clear permissions, observable traces, and robust evaluation under real workloads.

blogList.title: CommunicFlow v2: Separating the Messenger Without Rewriting the Product

desc.title: The constraint
desc.description: CommunicFlow V1 already carried core business domains: organisations, members, events, reclamations, and messaging. Realtime traffic was the pressure point. The v2 goal was pragmatic: isolate the messenger so chat load, WebRTC signaling, and presence would not destabilize the main REST application.
list: Keep business domains stable.
Isolate realtime concerns.
Share auth deliberately, not by duplication.
Operate on a VPS with simple, reliable tooling.

desc.title: A deployable boundary
desc.description: v2 uses a React/Vite SPA, an Express REST API, and a separate GraphQL/Socket.IO messenger service. GraphQL handles typed reads/mutations; Socket.IO handles primary realtime transport. Redis backs shared session state; internal service calls use constant-time service-key checks.

desc.title: Security as design
desc.description: Access and refresh tokens live in HTTP-only cookies with HS512, rotation, and DB revocation. TOTP 2FA, backup codes, and Cloudflare Turnstile protect sensitive flows. A session-level active organisation and super-admin exception make multi-tenant scope explicit.
desc.note: Security controls were part of architecture decisions, not post-launch patches.

desc.title: Realtime with rules
desc.description: The messenger supports rooms, presence, typing indicators, read receipts, and bounded history pagination. Call signaling uses STUN and short-lived HMAC TURN credentials through coturn, gated by organisation policy and discussion role. Realtime features are permissioned product behavior, not just sockets.

desc.title: Business modules still matter
desc.description: v2 also shipped a governed Drive with access-checked serving, trash, versions, activity trail, tokenized share links, and ZIP export. Events store recurrence rules and expand on read with defined horizon/cap. Reclamations run through an SLA job; notifications support preferences, grouping, and realtime delivery.

desc.title: Delivery gates
desc.description: Docker Compose runs behind nginx with TLS, security headers, real-IP handling, and WebSocket support. An eight-stage Jenkins pipeline validates Compose config, snapshots images, polls health checks, runs smoke verification, and retains rollback images. No Kubernetes/Prometheus stack was required for the target VPS scale.
list: Compose config validation.
Image build and snapshot.
Health checks and smoke tests.
Rollback image retention.

desc.title: What the split bought
desc.description: The messenger can fail, restart, or scale without taking the core workspace down. Auth and scope are shared deliberately. The hard part was not framework choice but keeping permissions, notifications, and deployment discipline consistent across the boundary.

blogList.title: Building a Local RAG Document Assistant: Ingestion, Retrieval, and Citations

desc.title: Why local-first RAG matters
desc.description: A document assistant is only useful when answers are traceable. Local-first RAG keeps sensitive documents under control while using models for synthesis. The core product rule: every answer should point to evidence, and missing evidence should be reported clearly.
list: Ingest and normalize documents.
Chunk with structure and metadata.
Embed and index for retrieval.
Generate answers with citations and refusal behavior.

desc.title: Ingestion pipeline
desc.description: Parse PDFs/DOCX/Markdown into clean text. Preserve headings, page numbers, document IDs, and access control metadata. Bad parsing creates bad retrieval no matter how good the model is. For scanned PDFs, OCR quality becomes part of system quality.

desc.title: Retrieval: vector + filters + reranking
desc.description: Use embeddings for semantic recall, but combine with metadata filters and optionally keyword search. Retrieve a candidate set, rerank, then pass only the most relevant chunks to the model. Always keep tenant/document access control in the retrieval query.

code.content:
SELECT id, doc_id, page, text
FROM document_chunks
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 8;

desc.note: The most common RAG bug is retrieving plausible but unauthorized or irrelevant context.

desc.title: Citations and prompt discipline
desc.description: Ask the model to answer only from provided context and include source IDs. Render citations in UI so users can verify. When context is insufficient, the assistant should say so and suggest what document is missing.

desc.title: Evaluation and production concerns
desc.description: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Track recall@k, groundedness, citation accuracy, latency, and cost. Log source IDs and model versions. Protect against prompt injection inside documents by treating retrieved text as data, not instructions.

blogList.title: AI Agents in Production in 2026: RAG, Tool Use, Evals, and Guardrails

desc.title: From demo agents to dependable systems
desc.description: The 2026 agent landscape has moved from prompt demos to workflow systems. The useful question is no longer "can the model call a tool?" but "can the system complete a bounded task reliably, safely, and at a predictable cost?" Production agents work best when the model is one component inside a deterministic workflow: explicit state, typed tools, retrieval, policy checks, and human escalation paths.
list: Model: reasoning and language generation, not the source of truth.
Tools: narrow contracts with schemas, idempotency, and audit logs.
State: persisted task state so retries and handoffs are observable.
Policy: authorization and data boundaries enforced outside the prompt.
desc.note: A practical rule: give the agent autonomy only where you can measure correctness and reverse or contain mistakes.

desc.title: RAG is a retrieval system, not a vector database
desc.description: Retrieval-Augmented Generation works when retrieval quality is treated as an engineering problem. Chunking, metadata, filters, reranking, and citation rendering matter as much as the embedding model. For enterprise or documentation assistants, the answer should be grounded in retrieved passages and expose where each claim came from.

desc.title: Tool contracts and guardrails
desc.description: Every tool exposed to an agent should have a schema, permission model, timeout, and side-effect classification. Read-only tools can be broader; mutating tools should be narrow and auditable. Guardrails are not just prompt text — they are validation, allowlists, rate limits, and approval gates before irreversible actions.

desc.title: Evaluation is the release gate
desc.description: In 2026, teams that ship agents responsibly run offline evals before every model, prompt, or retrieval change. An eval set should include real user tasks, adversarial inputs, tool failures, and stale-context cases. Score task success, groundedness, citation accuracy, refusal quality, and cost/latency. Traces from production should feed new eval cases.
list: Task success: did the workflow produce the expected outcome?
Groundedness: are claims supported by retrieved sources?
Safety: did the agent respect permissions and refusal policies?
Efficiency: tokens, tool calls, latency, and cost per successful task.

desc.title: Cost, latency, and observability
desc.description: Agent cost is multiplicative: retrieval, model calls, tool calls, retries, and long contexts add up. Use model routing for simple steps, cache embeddings and retrieval results where valid, cap iterations, and stream user-visible progress. Observability should capture prompts, tool inputs/outputs, retrieved source IDs, token usage, and final decisions — with redaction for sensitive data.
desc.note: The best production metric is not "agent answered" but "user completed a verified task within budget and policy".

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: The scientific and engineering direction is clear: agentic systems improve when they are constrained by retrieval, evaluation, and policy. The winning pattern is hybrid — deterministic software for control, models for language and planning, and humans for high-risk decisions.

blogList.title: AI-Assisted Software Engineering in 2026: Productivity, Code Quality, and Security

desc.title: The shift from autocomplete to agentic development
desc.description: By 2026, AI coding tools are no longer just autocomplete. They can draft tests, refactor modules, explain failures, generate migration scripts, and propose pull requests. The productivity gain is real when tasks are well-scoped, but the engineering responsibility does not move. Teams still own correctness, security, maintainability, and operational behavior.
list: Good fit: boilerplate, tests, refactors, documentation, migrations.
Risky fit: auth, cryptography, billing, concurrency, security boundaries.
Best practice: small diffs, strong tests, and human review.

desc.title: A review checklist for AI-generated code
desc.description: Generated code should pass the same bar as human code, plus extra skepticism. Reviewers should check assumptions, missing edge cases, dependency choices, and whether the code matches existing project conventions. AI often produces plausible code; plausibility is not correctness.

code.content:
## AI diff review checklist
- [ ] Does it solve the reported problem?
- [ ] Are inputs validated and errors handled?
- [ ] Does it follow existing patterns and naming?
- [ ] Are tests meaningful, not just passing?
- [ ] Any new dependency, secret, or permission?
- [ ] Any security, privacy, or performance regression?

desc.title: Testing as the safety net
desc.description: AI-assisted development increases the value of tests. Unit tests catch local regressions, integration tests verify contracts, and end-to-end tests protect user flows. When an agent generates code, ask it to generate tests too — then review the tests critically. A weak test suite can create false confidence.

desc.title: Security and provenance
desc.description: AI tools can accidentally introduce vulnerable patterns, copy insecure defaults, or suggest packages with weak maintenance. Combine AI use with SAST, dependency scanning, secret scanning, and SBOM/provenance practices. For sensitive domains, require threat modeling and explicit human approval.
desc.note: The right metric is not lines generated. It is validated outcomes delivered safely.

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: AI-assisted engineering is a multiplier for disciplined teams. The science is in evaluation and human factors; the craft is in code review, testing, and secure delivery. Teams that invest in guardrails get speed without trading away quality.

blogList.title: Browser AI in 2026: WebGPU, Local Inference, and Privacy-Preserving UX

desc.title: Why local inference is back on the table
desc.description: Cloud LLMs are powerful, but not every AI feature needs a remote round trip. In 2026, browser and on-device inference are practical for selected tasks: classification, embeddings, speech features, image preprocessing, summarization of small local content, and assistive UI. The benefits are latency, offline resilience, and better privacy boundaries when data stays on device.
list: Low-latency interactions for small models.
Reduced data transfer for sensitive content.
Offline or degraded-network capability.
Hybrid fallback to cloud models for heavy tasks.

desc.title: WebGPU and the browser runtime
desc.description: WebGPU gives web applications more direct access to modern GPU capabilities than WebGL-era compute hacks. It enables better performance for ML workloads, graphics, and parallel compute. The engineering challenge is capability detection, fallback paths, memory limits, and thermal/mobile constraints.

desc.title: Hybrid AI UX patterns
desc.description: The best browser AI features are often hybrid. Use local inference for instant feedback, redaction, or drafting; escalate to a server model for complex reasoning or large context. Be transparent in the UI about where processing happens, especially for sensitive data.
desc.note: Privacy-preserving UX is not just a backend decision. Users should understand whether text, audio, or files leave their device.

desc.title: Performance and model selection
desc.description: Small models require careful product design. Define the task narrowly, measure quality against a baseline, and budget for startup/download time. Quantized models can reduce size, but you must evaluate accuracy loss. For scientific and production use, publish eval criteria, not just demos.

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: Browser AI is not replacing cloud AI; it is expanding the design space. The winning products choose the right runtime per task, measure quality, and make privacy/performance tradeoffs visible.

blogList.title: Responsible AI Engineering in 2026: EU AI Act, Risk Management, and Technical Controls

desc.title: Regulation meets engineering practice
desc.description: In 2026, responsible AI is no longer only a policy document. The EU AI Act phased timeline and global AI governance frameworks push teams to translate principles into technical controls. For engineers, this means data provenance, model documentation, human oversight, logging, evaluation, and clear user communication become product requirements.
list: Classify the AI use case and risk level early.
Document data sources, intended use, and limits.
Design human oversight for high-impact decisions.
Log decisions and monitor for drift or misuse.

desc.title: Technical controls developers can implement
desc.description: Responsible AI starts in the architecture. Limit data collection, redact sensitive inputs, separate system prompts from untrusted content, and keep audit trails. For RAG and agents, store source IDs and tool traces. For user-facing AI, label outputs as AI-generated where appropriate and provide feedback channels.

desc.title: Evaluation beyond accuracy
desc.description: Scientific evaluation for AI systems should include robustness, bias where relevant, prompt-injection resilience, privacy leakage, and failure behavior. A model can score well on benchmark accuracy and still be unsafe in a real workflow. Use red-team tests, domain eval sets, and production monitoring.
desc.note: For high-impact systems, "unknown failure mode" is itself a risk to document and mitigate.

desc.title: Human oversight and product UX
desc.description: Human-in-the-loop is not a checkbox. The interface must make review possible: show evidence, confidence limits, source citations, and an easy correction path. Users should know when they are interacting with AI and what the system can and cannot do.

code.content:
ai_feature:
  name: support_reply_draft
  risk: limited
  human_review: required_before_send
  data:
    pii_redaction: enabled
    retention_days: 30
  monitoring:
    - hallucination_reports
    - unsafe_output_flags
    - user_feedback_rate

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: Responsible AI is an engineering discipline: governance translated into systems. Teams that build provenance, evaluation, and oversight into the lifecycle will move faster because they avoid costly trust failures later.

blogList.title: Platform Engineering in 2026: Building an Internal Developer Platform That Teams Actually Use

desc.title: Why platform engineering became a 2026 priority
desc.description: As systems grew into microservices, cloud accounts, Kubernetes clusters, observability stacks, and AI workloads, cognitive load became a delivery bottleneck. Platform engineering addresses this by productizing infrastructure: an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) provides paved roads so product teams can ship without reinventing CI/CD, deployment, secrets, and observability for every service.
list: Golden paths for common service types.
Self-service environments and deployments.
Built-in security, observability, and cost controls.
Documentation and support treated as product features.

desc.title: Golden paths over golden cages
desc.description: A good platform makes the right thing easy, not the only thing possible. Provide templates for common workloads — web API, worker, frontend, scheduled job — with sensible defaults. Teams should be able to extend or escape the path when they have a real need, but the default should cover most cases.

code.content:
# service.yaml - developer-facing platform contract
name: billing-api
owner: team-payments
runtime: node20
type: web
exposure: internal
resources:
  postgres: true
  redis: false
observability:
  logs: true
  metrics: true
  traces: true
deploy:
  strategy: rolling
  environments: [staging, production]

desc.title: The platform as a product
desc.description: Internal platforms fail when they are built as a side project with no users. Treat developers as customers: measure onboarding time, deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and time to restore. Collect feedback, maintain docs, and version platform APIs. A platform that is technically impressive but hard to use will be bypassed.
desc.note: Adoption is the main KPI. A paved road nobody takes is technical debt with branding.

desc.title: Security and policy by default
desc.description: The IDP should embed policy: secret scanning, dependency scanning, SAST, image provenance, least-privilege IAM, and environment guardrails. Developers should get secure defaults without filing tickets. Policy-as-code makes these controls reviewable and testable.

desc.title: AI workloads change the platform
desc.description: In 2026, IDPs increasingly need to support model gateways, vector stores, GPU scheduling, prompt/eval pipelines, and data governance. The platform should provide approved model endpoints, logging/redaction, cost quotas, and evaluation hooks so teams can build AI features without each team creating its own shadow AI stack.
list: Model gateway with auth, rate limits, and usage tracking.
Secrets and PII redaction in prompt/response logs.
Evaluation pipeline for prompts, RAG, and agents.
Cost budgets per team or feature.

desc.title: Takeaway
desc.description: Platform engineering is not about adding another tool. It is about reducing cognitive load while increasing reliability, security, and speed. The best IDP is boring in the right places: predictable deployments, visible ownership, and safe defaults.

blogList.title: Software Supply Chain Security in 2026: SBOMs, Signing, Provenance, and CI Controls

desc.title: Why supply chain security is now baseline engineering
desc.description: Modern applications depend on hundreds of direct and transitive dependencies, container base images, GitHub Actions, package registries, and build systems. Supply chain security is no longer a specialist concern; it is part of normal software delivery. The 2026 baseline is: know what you ship, verify where it came from, and detect tampering before deployment.
list: SBOM generation for applications and containers.
Dependency and vulnerability scanning in CI.
Artifact signing and provenance attestations.
Least-privilege CI tokens and protected release workflows.

desc.title: SBOMs make dependencies visible
desc.description: A Software Bill of Materials lists components, versions, licenses, and relationships. It does not fix vulnerabilities by itself, but it makes response possible. When a new CVE is disclosed, teams with SBOMs can quickly answer: are we affected, where, and in which deployed artifact?

code.content:
# Generate an SBOM for a container image
syft ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json

# Scan the SBOM for known vulnerabilities
grype sbom:sbom.spdx.json --fail-on high

desc.note: Treat SBOM generation as a build artifact, not a one-time audit document.

desc.title: Signing and provenance
desc.description: Signing proves that an artifact was produced by a trusted identity. Provenance proves how it was built: which repo, commit, workflow, and builder produced it. Together they reduce the risk of tampered images or packages reaching production. Use immutable digests in deployment manifests, not floating tags.

code.content:
# Sign a container image by digest
cosign sign ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:3f...

# Verify signature before deployment
cosign verify ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:3f...   --certificate-identity-regexp "https://github.com/acme/api/.*"   --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"

desc.title: CI/CD hardening
desc.description: Many supply chain incidents enter through CI. Pin action versions by SHA, restrict workflow permissions, separate build and deploy credentials, and protect release branches/tags. Pull request workflows should not expose production secrets. Dependency updates should be reviewed like code, especially for packages with install scripts or broad permissions.
list: Pin GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs.
Use `permissions:` with least privilege in workflows.
Require reviews for dependency and workflow changes.
Keep build provenance and logs for incident response.

desc.title: AI-generated code and dependency risk
desc.description: AI coding assistants accelerate delivery, but they can also suggest outdated packages, insecure defaults, or nonexistent dependencies. In 2026, secure teams pair AI-assisted development with policy checks: dependency allowlists where appropriate, SAST, secret scanning, and human review for security-sensitive changes.
desc.note: Speed from AI is real; so is the need for verification. Treat generated code as untrusted until reviewed and tested.

desc.title: Takeaway
desc.description: Supply chain security is a system property. SBOMs provide visibility, signing provides integrity, provenance provides trust, and CI hardening reduces the attack surface. The goal is not zero dependencies — it is controlled, observable dependencies.

blogList.title: Core Web Vitals in 2026: INP, RUM, and Performance Engineering That Users Feel

desc.title: Why INP changed frontend priorities
desc.description: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) made responsiveness a first-class metric. It captures interaction latency across the page lifecycle, not only the first input. In 2026, frontend performance means fast initial render, fast response to input, and visual stability under real conditions.
list: LCP: main content appears quickly.
INP: UI responds quickly to interactions.
CLS: layout remains stable.
TTFB/latency: backend still matters.

desc.title: Lab + field measurement
desc.description: Use Lighthouse/DevTools for diagnosis and RUM for reality. Field data varies by device class, browser, extensions, network, and user behavior. Prioritize by real-user impact, not just local scores.

desc.title: How to improve INP
desc.description: Long tasks block interaction. Break heavy work into chunks, defer third-party scripts, avoid unnecessary rerenders, and use virtualization for large lists. Profile interactions that users actually perform: filter, open modal, submit form, switch tab.
desc.note: Optimizing a metric without improving user-perceived flow is wasted effort. Measure before and after with the same interaction.

desc.title: LCP and CLS fundamentals
desc.description: Optimize LCP by serving critical images efficiently, reducing render-blocking resources, and caching HTML/data where possible. Prevent CLS by reserving space for images, embeds, fonts, and dynamic banners. Avoid inserting content above existing content after load.
list: Set width/height or aspect-ratio for media.
Use font-display and limit font variants.
Preload truly critical assets only.
Avoid layout-shifting ads/banners.

desc.title: Performance budgets in CI
desc.description: Make performance regressions visible. Add bundle budgets, Lighthouse CI for key pages, and RUM dashboards with alerts. Performance is not a one-time sprint; it is an engineering habit tied to product quality and SEO.

blogList.title: FinOps for Developers in 2026: Cloud Cost as an Engineering Metric

desc.title: Why FinOps is engineering work
desc.description: Cloud cost is not just a finance report - it is the result of architecture, scaling policies, data retention, and feature design. In 2026, AI workloads, observability pipelines, and always-on environments make cost visibility critical. FinOps aligns engineering, product, and finance around measurable tradeoffs.
list: Make cost visible by team, service, and environment.
Tie spend to business outcomes.
Detect anomalies early.
Optimize continuously, not once a quarter.

desc.title: Tagging and allocation
desc.description: You cannot optimize what you cannot attribute. Enforce resource tagging for owner, service, environment, and cost center. For shared platforms, define allocation rules. Without allocation, cost discussions become political instead of technical.

code.content:
tags:
  service: billing-api
  team: payments
  env: production
  cost_center: eng-platform
  managed_by: terraform

desc.title: Architecture levers
desc.description: Right-size compute, use autoscaling, schedule non-prod environments, and choose storage classes intentionally. Avoid over-fetching logs/metrics with no retention plan. For AI features, track token usage, context size, caching hit rate, and model choice per task.
desc.note: The cheapest model is not always the lowest total cost if it causes retries, bad answers, or human rework.

desc.title: Budgets, alerts, and governance
desc.description: Set budgets per team or product area and alert on forecasted overrun, not only month-end totals. Use guardrails: instance size limits, idle resource cleanup, and approval for expensive resources. Make cost part of design reviews.
list: Budget alerts at 50/80/100%.
Anomaly detection for sudden spend spikes.
Cleanup policies for orphaned volumes/snapshots.
Cost review in architecture decision records.

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: FinOps maturity means engineers understand the cost impact of their decisions. The goal is not minimal spend; it is efficient spend that supports reliability, speed, and user value.

blogList.title: Edge and Serverless in 2026: Choosing the Right Execution Model

desc.title: No single runtime wins everywhere
desc.description: Edge functions, serverless platforms, containers, and long-running services are tools with different constraints. The right choice depends on latency, state, cold starts, execution duration, data locality, cost, and team operations. In 2026, hybrid architectures are normal.
list: Edge: close to users, limited runtime/APIs.
Serverless: elastic, event-driven, possible cold starts.
Containers: portable and predictable for long-running workloads.
Managed services: reduce ops when constraints fit.

desc.title: When edge makes sense
desc.description: Use edge for latency-sensitive, stateless logic: auth gating, routing, A/B flags, personalization headers, simple cache decisions. Keep it close to data sources where possible; edge compute far from its database can negate latency gains.

desc.title: When serverless makes sense
desc.description: Serverless is strong for bursty workloads: webhooks, image processing, scheduled jobs, async pipelines. Watch cold starts, concurrency limits, timeout limits, and observability. Package size and initialization code directly affect startup latency.
desc.note: Serverless removes server management, not system design. You still need idempotency, retries, dead-letter queues, and monitoring.

desc.title: Containers and long-running services
desc.description: Use containers/services for stateful connections, long-running workers, heavy dependencies, custom networking, or predictable high throughput. Kubernetes is powerful but operationally expensive; choose it when workload complexity justifies it.

code.content:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: worker }
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: ghcr.io/acme/worker:1.8.0
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "200m", memory: "256Mi" }
            limits: { cpu: "1", memory: "512Mi" }

desc.title: Decision checklist
desc.description: Choose by constraints: latency target, data locality, execution time, statefulness, traffic pattern, team maturity, and cost model. Measure with realistic load. The best architecture is the simplest one that meets SLOs and can be operated by your team.

blogList.title: Realtime Architecture with GraphQL Subscriptions, Redis, and Socket.IO

desc.title: Realtime features need explicit boundaries
desc.description: Chat, notifications, presence, and collaboration features look simple in demos but become complex at scale. You need clear contracts for event names, payloads, ordering, delivery expectations, and authorization. Start by defining which events must be durable, which can be ephemeral, and which require acknowledgment.
list: Ephemeral: typing indicators, presence heartbeats.
Durable: messages, notifications, audit-relevant events.
Ordered per room/channel: chat messages.
Idempotent consumers: handle duplicate deliveries safely.

desc.title: GraphQL subscriptions and transport
desc.description: GraphQL subscriptions are great for typed realtime data, but transport and scaling matter. WebSockets keep persistent connections; you need heartbeats, backpressure awareness, and reconnect logic. In some systems, Socket.IO handles realtime transport while GraphQL handles typed queries/mutations.

desc.title: Redis as the realtime backbone
desc.description: Redis Pub/Sub is useful for fanout across instances; Streams or durable queues are better when you need replay or delivery tracking. Use Redis to coordinate presence, rate limits, and transient state, but persist source-of-truth data in a database.
desc.note: Pub/Sub does not guarantee durable delivery to offline consumers. Use Streams/queues when missed events matter.

desc.title: Authorization and scale
desc.description: Every subscription/room join must be authorized at connect and at event time. Do not trust client-provided room IDs blindly. Plan for horizontal scaling with sticky sessions or shared adapters, and observe connection count, event lag, dropped messages, and memory usage.
list: Authenticate socket on handshake.
Authorize room membership per event.
Rate limit noisy events (typing, presence).
Set payload size limits and timeouts.

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: Realtime architecture is about correctness under concurrency. Choose the right durability model, enforce authorization on every boundary, and make event flows observable. Simple, explicit event contracts beat clever but opaque abstractions.

blogList.title: Secure Authentication in 2026: HTTP-only Cookies, OAuth2, 2FA, and Abuse Protection

desc.title: Authentication is a system, not a login form
desc.description: Secure authentication combines credential handling, session lifecycle, MFA, abuse prevention, and recovery flows. Most breaches come from weak defaults: long-lived tokens, missing rate limits, poor recovery, or tokens exposed to JavaScript. Design auth as a threat-modeled system.
list: Use HTTPS everywhere; secure cookies in production.
Short-lived access tokens, rotating refresh tokens.
MFA for sensitive accounts/actions.
Rate limit, audit, and monitor auth events.

desc.title: HTTP-only cookies and token lifecycle
desc.description: Storing tokens in HTTP-only, Secure, SameSite cookies reduces XSS token theft risk compared to localStorage. Access tokens should be short-lived; refresh tokens should rotate and be revocable server-side. On refresh reuse or anomaly, revoke the session family.
desc.note: Cookie flags reduce risk; they do not replace CSRF protection, input validation, or XSS prevention.

desc.title: OAuth2/OIDC for delegated identity
desc.description: Use OAuth2/OIDC when users authenticate through an identity provider. Validate state, nonce, issuer, audience, signature, and token expiry. Never trust frontend-only identity claims. Map external identities to local users carefully to avoid account-linking vulnerabilities.

desc.title: 2FA, recovery, and abuse protection
desc.description: TOTP-based 2FA improves account security, but recovery flows are often the weakest link. Backup codes must be hashed, one-time, and auditable. Protect login/signup/reset endpoints with rate limits, bot protection (e.g., Turnstile), and anomaly detection.
list: Hash backup codes; show once; allow regeneration.
Notify users on password/MFA/email changes.
Apply step-up auth for sensitive actions.
Log auth events with privacy-aware metadata.

desc.title: 2026 takeaway
desc.description: Modern auth is defense in depth. Choose boring, proven primitives; validate every token; monitor abuse; and make recovery secure. The best auth UX is clear and safe, not clever.

blogList.title: Progressive Web Apps in 2026: Offline, Installability, and Performance Tradeoffs

desc.title: What a PWA is - and is not
desc.description: A Progressive Web App is a web application that uses modern browser capabilities to deliver a reliable, installable, app-like experience. It is not a replacement for every native app. PWAs shine when reach, instant updates, and web distribution matter; native apps still win for deep OS integration, advanced background tasks, or heavy device-specific capabilities.
list: Reliable: loads with poor network or offline when cached.
Fast: optimized rendering and interaction.
Installable: manifest + service worker criteria met.
Engaging: can use push/notifications where appropriate and permitted.

desc.title: The web app manifest
desc.description: The manifest declares how the app appears when installed: name, icons, theme color, display mode, and start URL. Keep icons complete and ensure the start URL works offline or degrades gracefully.

desc.title: Service worker caching strategies
desc.description: Service workers sit between the app and network. The right caching strategy depends on the resource type. Static assets can be cache-first; API requests often need network-first or stale-while-revalidate with clear freshness rules. Cache invalidation must be planned - stale assets are a common PWA failure mode.

desc.title: Offline UX and data sync
desc.description: Offline support is more than caching a shell. Decide what users can read, edit, or queue while offline. For forms and mutations, store intent locally and sync when connectivity returns. Be explicit in the UI about sync state to avoid data-loss surprises.
desc.note: Do not promise offline behavior you cannot guarantee. A clear 'saved locally, will sync' state is better than silent failure.

desc.title: Performance, security, and 2026 reality
desc.description: PWAs still require HTTPS, careful permission use, and performance discipline. In 2026, installability criteria and platform support vary by browser/OS, so test on target devices. Pair PWA features with Core Web Vitals, accessibility, and normal web security practices.

blogList.title: Software Testing Essentials: Strategy, Automation, and Confidence in 2026

desc.title: Testing is a risk strategy
desc.description: The purpose of testing is not 100% coverage. It is confidence that important behaviors work and regressions are caught early. Good test suites balance speed, signal, and maintenance cost.

desc.title: The practical test pyramid
desc.description: Use many fast unit tests for pure logic, fewer integration tests for boundaries, and a small number of end-to-end tests for critical user journeys. Contract tests are valuable when services evolve independently.
list: Unit: fast, isolated, deterministic.
Integration: DB, API, queue, filesystem boundaries.
E2E: login, checkout, publish, critical flows.
Contract: provider/consumer compatibility.

desc.title: Make tests deterministic
desc.description: Flaky tests destroy trust. Control time, randomness, network, and external dependencies. In CI, rerun flakiness detection but treat flaky tests as bugs, not normal noise.

desc.title: CI as a quality gate
desc.description: Run tests on every pull request, keep feedback fast, and publish artifacts like coverage and test reports. For AI-assisted code, tests are even more important because generated code can be plausible but subtly wrong.
desc.note: A failing test should explain behavior. Prefer clear assertions over clever abstractions.

desc.title: 2026 perspective
desc.description: AI can generate tests, but humans must review intent. The best teams use AI to expand coverage quickly, then curate tests for business meaning and maintainability.

blogList.title: Docker for Developers: Images, Compose, Security, and Production Habits

desc.title: Containers solve environment drift
desc.description: Docker packages an app with its runtime dependencies so it runs consistently across developer machines, CI, and servers. The container is not a VM; it shares the host kernel and should be treated as an immutable runtime unit.

desc.title: A good Dockerfile is small and predictable
desc.description: Use minimal base images, pin versions, leverage layer caching, and run as a non-root user. Multi-stage builds keep build tools out of runtime images.

code.content:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
USER node
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

desc.title: Compose for local integration
desc.description: Docker Compose is ideal for local stacks: app, database, cache, and observability tools. Keep it close to production topology, but do not confuse local convenience with production orchestration.

code.content:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    env_file: [.env]
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes: [db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
volumes:
  db_data:

desc.title: Security basics
desc.description: Scan images, avoid secrets in layers, pin base image digests where possible, and limit capabilities. Containers improve packaging, not trust boundaries by default.
desc.note: Never put API keys in Dockerfile ARG/ENV for production images; inject them at runtime through a secret manager or environment injection.

desc.title: 2026 perspective
desc.description: Containers remain foundational, but supply chain controls are now expected: SBOMs, signed images, provenance, and vulnerability gates in CI.

blogList.title: GraphQL vs REST: A Practical Decision Guide for Modern APIs

desc.title: The real question is not 'which is better'
desc.description: GraphQL and REST solve overlapping but different problems. REST models resources through URLs and HTTP semantics; GraphQL models a typed schema and lets clients query exactly the fields they need. The right choice depends on client diversity, caching needs, team maturity, and operational constraints.
list: REST: simple, cache-friendly, excellent HTTP tooling.
GraphQL: flexible queries, strong typing, single endpoint.
Hybrid: common in real systems - REST for simple resources, GraphQL for composition.

desc.title: REST strengths
desc.description: REST works well when resources are clear and HTTP semantics map naturally: GET for reads, POST for creation, PUT/PATCH for updates, DELETE for removal. CDNs, browser caches, proxies, and observability tools understand REST patterns out of the box.

code.content:
GET /v1/projects/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60
ETag: "p42-v3"

desc.title: GraphQL strengths
desc.description: GraphQL reduces over-fetching and under-fetching when multiple clients need different views of the same domain. It is especially useful for dashboards, mobile apps, and aggregation layers. But flexibility shifts complexity to the server: query cost, N+1 problems, and authorization per field.

desc.title: Security and performance pitfalls
desc.description: REST endpoints can be rate-limited by route; GraphQL needs query depth/complexity limits because one request can be expensive. Both need authentication, authorization, input validation, and audit logging. In GraphQL, never rely on hiding fields in the UI - enforce authorization in resolvers/data loaders.
desc.note: Authorize by business object/field, not by query shape. A flexible query language increases the need for strict server-side rules.

desc.title: 2026 recommendation
desc.description: Use REST by default for simple, cacheable resource APIs and public integrations. Use GraphQL when client composition is the main pain and you have the tooling for schema governance, query cost control, and observability. Many mature platforms use both.

blogList.title: SEO for Developer Portfolios in 2026: Technical Foundations, Content, and Credibility

desc.title: SEO starts with technical correctness
desc.description: For developer portfolios, SEO is less about tricks and more about making your work understandable to crawlers and useful to humans. Crawlable pages, clean URLs, canonical tags, proper metadata, sitemap/robots, and fast rendering are the baseline. If search engines cannot reliably discover and render your pages, content quality won't matter.
list: Unique title/description per page.
Canonical URL and hreflang for multilingual sites.
XML sitemap + robots.txt.
No accidental noindex on production.

desc.title: Structured data and entity clarity
desc.description: Schema.org helps search engines understand who you are and what a page represents. For a portfolio, Person, WebSite, ProfilePage, Article, and BreadcrumbList are useful. Keep data truthful and consistent with visible page content.

code.content:
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Person",
  "name": "Mohamed Achraf Ben Fredj",
  "url": "https://ach02raf.pro/en",
  "sameAs": [
    "https://github.com/ach02raf",
    "https://www.linkedin.com/in/ach02raf/"
  ],
  "jobTitle": "Web, Mobile, DevOps & AI Engineer"
}

desc.title: Performance and Core Web Vitals
desc.description: Search systems consider page experience signals. Fast LCP, responsive INP, and stable CLS improve user experience and reduce bounce. Optimize images, fonts, JS payload, and rendering strategy. Static generation is excellent for portfolio/blog pages when content is known at build time.
desc.note: Don't chase a perfect Lighthouse score at the expense of real user experience. Use lab tools for debugging and field data for decisions.

desc.title: Content that demonstrates expertise
desc.description: A portfolio ranks better when it proves competence. Write case studies with problem, constraints, architecture, tradeoffs, and outcomes. For blogs, prefer specific technical depth over generic AI-generated summaries. Show code, diagrams in text form, decisions, and lessons learned.
list: Case studies: context, role, stack, decisions, impact.
Blogs: practical problem, explanation, code, pitfalls.
Projects: live/demo/source links when available.
Keep content updated when tech or your role changes.

desc.title: International SEO for FR/EN/DE
desc.description: Multilingual portfolios need consistent language mapping. Use `hreflang`, localized metadata, and language-specific URLs. Avoid automatic redirects that prevent crawlers/users from choosing language. Ensure each locale has meaningful content, not just machine-translated labels.

blogList.title: TypeScript for Professional Teams: Types, Validation, and Maintainable APIs

desc.title: TypeScript is a design tool, not just syntax
desc.description: TypeScript's value is not adding colons everywhere. It makes contracts explicit: function inputs, API responses, domain models, and component props. Used well, it reduces runtime bugs and improves refactoring confidence. Used poorly, it creates fake safety through `any`, unsafe casts, and duplicated types.
list: Model domain types close to business concepts.
Prefer unknown over any at boundaries.
Validate external data at runtime.
Keep types simple and composable.

desc.title: Types at boundaries, validation at runtime
desc.description: TypeScript types disappear at runtime. Any data from HTTP, files, env vars, localStorage, or user input must be validated. Use schema validation (Zod, Valibot, etc.) to parse unknown input into trusted typed data.

desc.title: API contracts and discriminated unions
desc.description: Discriminated unions model states clearly: loading/success/error, payment states, workflow steps. They force exhaustive handling and make illegal states harder to represent.

desc.title: Team practices that keep TS healthy
desc.description: Enable strict mode, avoid broad type assertions, and lint for unsafe patterns. Prefer generated types from OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas when possible. Keep DTOs separate from domain models when external contracts differ from internal behavior.
desc.note: A `as SomeType` cast is often a smell at system boundaries. Parse, don't assert.

desc.title: 2026 perspective
desc.description: TypeScript remains the default for large JavaScript codebases. The trend is stronger runtime validation, better type inference, schema-driven contracts, and AI-assisted refactors guarded by tests and strict typing.

blogList.title: DevOps in 2026: CI/CD, Observability, Platform Thinking, and Reliable Delivery

desc.title: DevOps as an operating model
desc.description: DevOps is not a toolchain; it is the practice of reducing friction between building software and running it. In 2026, strong DevOps teams combine CI/CD, infrastructure as code, observability, security checks, and clear ownership. The goal is fast delivery with controlled risk.
list: Small, frequent changes.
Automated build/test/deploy pipelines.
Observable systems with actionable alerts.
Shared ownership of reliability.

desc.title: CI/CD with quality gates
desc.description: A pipeline should do more than deploy. It should validate formatting, tests, security scans, and build artifacts before release. Promotion between environments should be traceable to a commit and artifact.

code.content:
name: ci
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

desc.title: Observability: logs, metrics, traces
desc.description: You cannot operate what you cannot see. Logs explain events, metrics show trends, and traces connect requests across services. Alert on symptoms users feel — error rate, latency, saturation — before paging on every internal cause.
desc.note: An alert without a runbook is often just noise.

desc.title: Infrastructure as Code and GitOps
desc.description: Manage infrastructure through reviewed code. IaC makes environments reproducible; GitOps makes desired state visible in version control. This improves auditability and rollback confidence.

desc.title: 2026 direction
desc.description: DevOps is converging with platform engineering and AI-assisted operations. Teams use AI for incident summaries, anomaly detection, and runbook drafting, but keep humans and deterministic controls in the loop for risky changes.

blogList.title: React in 2026: Component Architecture, State, and Performance at Scale

desc.title: Modern React is about boundaries
desc.description: React is no longer just components and hooks. Professional React apps require clear boundaries: server vs client responsibilities, UI state vs server state, reusable primitives vs business components. The goal is predictable rendering, simple data flow, and maintainable code.
list: Keep components small and purpose-driven.
Separate data fetching/caching from presentation.
Colocate state where it is used.
Use TypeScript for prop and API contracts.

desc.title: State management: choose by state type
desc.description: Not all state is equal. Local UI state belongs in component state; shared UI state may need context or a small store; server state should use a data-fetching/cache layer. Overusing global stores creates coupling and rerender noise.

desc.title: Performance: measure before memoizing
desc.description: React performance issues usually come from unnecessary renders, heavy computations on the main thread, or oversized bundles. Use profiling tools first. Apply `memo`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback` where they solve a measured problem; premature memoization adds complexity.
desc.note: Memoization has a cost. It helps when it prevents expensive work or unstable props in hot paths.

desc.title: Component design for maintainability
desc.description: Design components around clear contracts. Prefer composition over prop explosion. Keep side effects in hooks or boundaries, and avoid hiding business rules deep in UI trees. Accessibility and keyboard behavior should be part of component design, not a late fix.

desc.title: 2026 perspective
desc.description: React ecosystems increasingly blend server rendering, streaming, islands/partial hydration patterns, and AI-assisted UI workflows. The fundamentals still win: clear state ownership, accessible UI, measured performance, and tested behavior.

blogList.title: Angular Performance in 2026: Change Detection, Rendering, and Real-User Metrics

desc.title: Performance starts with measurement
desc.description: Angular apps become slow for predictable reasons: too much change detection, large bundles, expensive templates, and unoptimized data flows. Before changing architecture, measure. Use Angular DevTools, browser performance traces, and Core Web Vitals field data to identify real bottlenecks.
list: Profile change detection and component render cost.
Measure LCP/INP/CLS in real users.
Audit bundle size and route-level loading.
Check API latency - frontend cannot fix slow backends alone.

desc.title: Change detection strategy
desc.description: Use `OnPush` where possible so components check only when inputs, async pipe emissions, or explicit signals/events require it. Prefer immutable data patterns or clear observable streams. Avoid expensive template functions; compute values in the component or via pure pipes.

desc.title: Routing, lazy loading, and defer
desc.description: Split large areas by route and load them only when needed. Angular standalone APIs and lazy routes reduce initial JS. For below-the-fold heavy UI, defer rendering until viewport or interaction when appropriate.

desc.title: Data flow and rendering discipline
desc.description: Use RxJS intentionally: avoid nested subscriptions, unsubscribe through async pipe or takeUntilDestroyed, and share expensive streams. Virtualize large lists, paginate server data, and keep templates simple. For forms and dashboards, debounce user-driven requests.
desc.note: A fast framework cannot compensate for rendering 5,000 DOM nodes on every keystroke.

desc.title: 2026 perspective
desc.description: Angular's modern direction - standalone components, signals, improved hydration and control flow - rewards teams that adopt explicit reactivity and clean boundaries. Performance is a product feature: budget it, monitor it, and regressions should fail CI where possible.

blogList.title: Design Patterns in Practice: SOLID, Composition, and Testable Architecture

desc.title: Why patterns should reduce complexity
desc.description: Design patterns are communication tools, not trophies. A pattern is useful when it makes change cheaper: adding a new payment provider, swapping storage, testing business logic without infrastructure. If a pattern adds indirection without reducing real complexity, it is accidental architecture.
list: Use patterns to isolate change points.
Prefer composition over inheritance.
Name abstractions after domain behavior.
Delete patterns that no longer pay for themselves.

desc.title: SOLID as practical guardrails
desc.description: SOLID works best as a smell detector. Single Responsibility keeps modules focused. Open/Closed encourages extension points around volatility. Liskov warns against broken substitutability. Interface Segregation avoids fat contracts. Dependency Inversion keeps business rules independent from frameworks and I/O.

desc.title: Strategy, Adapter, and Factory in real code
desc.description: Strategy replaces brittle conditionals when behavior varies by rule. Adapter isolates third-party APIs behind your contract. Factory centralizes creation when construction involves validation or environment selection. Avoid introducing them preemptively; refactor toward them when duplication or coupling appears.

desc.title: Testing the architecture
desc.description: Patterns should improve testability. Business rules can be unit tested with fake adapters. Integration tests verify real DB/HTTP boundaries. If tests require complex mocking of internals, the boundary may be wrong. Prefer testing behavior and contracts over implementation details.
desc.note: A good abstraction makes the fake implementation trivial.

desc.title: 2026 perspective
desc.description: With AI-generated code becoming common, architectural boundaries matter even more. Clear interfaces, domain naming, and tests help teams review generated changes safely. Patterns remain relevant when they make systems understandable to humans and verifiable by tools.
